paragraphs.text: i.e. Making wise, or giving instruction; for which purpose this psalm was composed by David (as it is most probable), or some other excellent prophet, for the use of the Church, which is haeres crucis, the heir of the cross, as Luther speaketh; and is here instructed how to carry herself under it, and to get benefit by it.
paragraphs.anchor: Maschil

paragraphs.text: i.e. We have both heard and heeded it, with utmost attention and affection. It is not a redundancy, but an emphasis that is here used.
paragraphs.anchor: We have heard with our ears

paragraphs.text: According to that they were commanded, Deu 6:1-10 and elsewhere, to whet good things upon their young children, and to propagate the memory of God’s noble acts to all posterity, Exo 12:26; Exo 13:14 Jos 4:6-7 Psa 78:4; Psa 78:6. Hear this, saith Basil, and blush, ye fathers, that neglect to teach your children. They made their mouths as it were books, wherein the noble acts of the Lord might be read to his praise, and to the drawing of their children’s hearts unto him.
paragraphs.anchor: Our fathers have told us

paragraphs.text: All which they faithfully related and carefully recorded, for the use of after ages. Psa 102:18, "This shall be written for the generation to come: and the people that shall be created shall praise the Lord."
paragraphs.anchor: What work thou didst

paragraphs.text: i.e. The Canaanites. These God, the great proprietary of all, supplanted, after that they had for a long time grown there as trees, and abounded with all kind of sensual delights, till they had filled the land from one end to the other with their uncleanness, Ezr 9:11.
paragraphs.anchor: How thou didst drive out the heathen

paragraphs.text: How thou didst afflict (or break in pieces) the people, and cast them out] Or, cause them (the Israelites) to spread and propagate (so Mollerus readeth it), as the vine sendeth out her branches.

Men are apt to arrogate to themselves, and say, as Luther hath it, Hoc ego feci. I made this, Sesostris, king of Egypt, when he had conquered any country, was wont to set up pillars, and thereupon to engrave these words, This land I got in possession by my own power, he was afterwards slain by his own servants (Herod. lib. 2).
paragraphs.anchor: For they got not the land in possession by their own sword, &c.

paragraphs.text: Quia per eam praelia et opera facta sunt, saith Kimchi. God is the great doer in all achievements.
paragraphs.anchor: But thy right hand

paragraphs.text: i.e. Illustris praesentia tua qua praeivisti et praeluxisti eis, thy gracious presence and conduct (Junius).
paragraphs.anchor: And the light of thy countenance

paragraphs.text: Free grace was the fundamental cause of all their felicity. God loved them because he loved them, Deu 7:7. He chose them of his love, and then loved them for his choice.
paragraphs.anchor: Because thou hadst a favour unto them

paragraphs.text: Heb. Thou art he, my King; Or, Thou art the same, my King, i.e. the same that thou wast to those of old. Oh, see to thy subjects, as ever thou hast done.
paragraphs.anchor: Thou art my King, O God

paragraphs.text: A Mandamus from thee will do it; he spake the word, and it was done. Some read it, Command deliverances, O Jacob; that is, O God of Jacob, as Psa 24:6.
paragraphs.anchor: Command deliverances for Jacob

paragraphs.text: Cornu petemus, a metaphor from horned creatures, as Deu 33:17. This we shall soon do if thou do but only give the word of command; for together with thy word goeth forth a power.
paragraphs.anchor: Through thee will we push down our enemies

paragraphs.text: Tuo nomine et numine, auspicio et ductu.
paragraphs.anchor: Through thy name

paragraphs.text: To trust in men or means is the ready road to utter ruin. Idas, one of the Argonauts, is brought in by the poet, bragging that he trusted not in the gods, but in his own arm and arms. αιια ουδε η οφελλει αιιευς τοσον οδατιον περ εμον δορυ.
paragraphs.anchor: For I will not trust in my bow

paragraphs.text: What need we to fear the Turks (said Sigismund, the young king of Hungary, in his pride and jollity), who need not at all to fear the falling of the heavens, which, if they should fall, yet were we able with our spears and halberds to hold them up for falling upon us? He shortly after this received a notable overthrow. Carnal confidence endeth in confusion.
Thou hast wrought and fought for us against those that sought to destroy us. Thou hast, and, therefore, thou will for thou art the same, my King, Psa 44:4.
paragraphs.anchor: But thou hast saved us

paragraphs.text: The Spaniards are said to be great boasters in the very lowest ebb of fortune. A godly man may be, and must be so by a holy gloriation; he must make his boasts of such a King, immortal, invisible, &c. The three children did so: Our God can deliver us, &c.
paragraphs.anchor: In God we boast all the day long

paragraphs.text: Thou alone shall have the praise of all our prosperity.
paragraphs.anchor: And praise thy name

paragraphs.text: Here is a sudden change, and a sad complaint, but handsomely brought in, the better to insinuate, the sooner to prevail for redress. Only this, it should have been remembered that the Lord’s hand was not shortened … but their iniquities had separated between them and their God, Isa 59:1-2. That noble General Trajan told Valens, the Arian emperor, that by warring against God he had abandoned the victory, and sent it to the enemies (Niceph. l. 11, c. 40).
paragraphs.anchor: But thou hast cut off, and put us to shame

paragraphs.text: By expectorating our faith and courage, and leaving us to a fearful faint heartedness, that flieth at the sound of a shaken leaf. God strengtheneth or weakeneth the arm of either army, Eze 30:24.
paragraphs.anchor: Thou makest us to turn back from the enemy

paragraphs.text: Aliqui occisi, dispersi alii, et venundati gratias, Some of us are slain, others scattered here and there, and sold for nought (Aben-Ezra).
paragraphs.anchor: Thou hast given us like sheep appointed for meat

paragraphs.text: Oh the many miseries of such a banishment! The poet Tyrtaeus thus expresses it:
paragraphs.anchor: And hast scattered us, &c.

paragraphs.text: Est miserum, patria amissa laribusque vagare:
Mendiea et timida voce rogare cibos.
Cum natisque errare suis, et coniuge moesta,
Et cum matre pia, cumque parente sene.
Thirty for a penny the Jews were sold by the Romans, saith Josephus, at the last devastation.
paragraphs.anchor: Thou sellest thy people for nought

paragraphs.text: Thou takest thy first chapman (as the pope gave England, in Henry VIIl’s time, Primo occupaluro, to him that could first seize it), and hast not made thy best of them; but given them away, for whom thou wast wont to give great nations, Isa 43:3. All the comfort in this case was, that yet they were dear to God as his sons, though sold for slaves to the enemies, as may be seen, Isa 50:1; Isa 52:3.
paragraphs.anchor: And dost not increase thy wealth by their price

paragraphs.text: This to a generous spirit is very grievous. The Cappadocians were noted for a servile people; and Tiberius said of his Romans, that they were homines ad servitutem parati men prepared for slavery, (Ammian. 1. 2). The Jews at this day hear ill among all nations for a nasty and sordid people. O Marcomanni, O Quades, O Sarmatae, tandem alios vobis deteriores inveni, said that emperor, O Marcomans, O Quades, O Sarmatians, I have at length found a more odious and contemptible people than you are any, meaning the Jews, with whose stench he was much annoyed.
paragraphs.anchor: Thou makest us a reproach to our neighbours

paragraphs.text: Who use to say, As base as a Jew, as wretched as an Israelite, &c. The Turks at this day say, Iudaeus sim si fallam, If I be not as good as my word, count me a very Jew. We use to say, As hard hearted as a Jew. Thus is fulfilled that which was threatened Deu 28:37 1Ki 9:7 Jer 24:9.
paragraphs.anchor: Thou makest us a byword among the heathen

paragraphs.text: Heb. All the day long, or every day; so as that there is neither hope of better nor place of worse.
paragraphs.anchor: My confusion is continually before me

paragraphs.text: Reproacheth religion, blasphemeth God and his people, as if he eared not what became of them; and his dispensation seemeth to say as much: this reflecteth upon the saints, and maketh them cry out -
paragraphs.anchor: For the voice of him that reproacheth and blasphemeth

paragraphs.text: - Pudet haec opprobria nobis,
Et dici potuisse, et non potuisse refelli.
This they allege, viz. their constance as an arguent of their sincerity, and a motive to pity. Apply this, with Jerome, to Christians, and then it is the voice of martyrs.
paragraphs.anchor: All this is come upon us; yet

paragraphs.text: ie. We have not relinquished the true religion, or revolted to dumb idols; but held us close to thy sincere service. And, therefore, if that heathen emperor going against his enemy could say, Non sic Deos coluimus ut ille nor vinceret, We have not so served the gods that they should serve us no better than to suffer us to be worsted (Antonin. Philosoph.); how much more may God’s faithful servants be confident of his help, and say, "All people will walk every one in the name of his god, and we will walk in the name of the Lord our God for ever and ever?" Mic 4:5.
paragraphs.anchor: Neither have we dealt falsely in thy covenant

paragraphs.text: Metaphora a stadio, saith Vatablus. As those that run a race stand not at a stay, much less turn back again; so neither have we either stopped or stepped backward, but advanced still toward the mark, having Nondum metam, We have not yet attained, for our motto, as St Paul had, Php 3:12; being in nothing terrified by our adversaries, nor afraid with any amazement, Php 1:28 1Pe 3:6.
paragraphs.anchor: Our heart is not turned back

paragraphs.text: We have watched over every particular action; God’s people are best when at worst.
paragraphs.anchor: Neither have our steps declined

paragraphs.text: i.e. In deserts haunted by dragons, see Isa 34:13; Isa 35:7, whereinto we are driven in banishment, and there hast crushed us, and covered us with the shadow of death, i.e. deadly calamity (Or. κακωσεως).
paragraphs.anchor: Though thou hast sore broken us in the place of dragons

paragraphs.text: i.e. Foregone our religion, as renegadoes, denying the Lord that bought us. In the time of the Maccabees many defected to Paganism; Demas, forsaking Paul, became an idolatrous priest at Thessalonica, saith Dorotheus; Julian turned Pagan; Damascen, Mahometan, as some write; Harding, an obstinate Papist. In the Palatinate, when, not forty years since, taken by the Spaniard, scarce one man in twenty stood out, but fell to Popery, as fast as leaves fall in antumn.
paragraphs.anchor: If we have forgotten the name of our God

paragraphs.text: This Ignatius, Laurentius, and thousands of those primitive Christians would die, rather than be drawn to do. So the three children, the seven brethren, &c. Origen, for yielding a little, was excommunicated.
paragraphs.anchor: Or stretched out our hands to a strange god

paragraphs.text: What pretences or excuses soever be used for the colouring and covering of the same.
paragraphs.anchor: Shall not God search this out?

paragraphs.text: See Mat 10:26, {See Trapp on "Mat 10:26"}
paragraphs.anchor: For he knoweth, &c.

paragraphs.text: q.d. Thou knowest that for thy sake, and not for vain glory, or out of pertinace, &c., we are killed. It is the cause, and not the punishment, that maketh the martyr. Some suffer as malefactors rather, Potes videre hominem morte affici, quare mortificetur nescis (Aug.).
paragraphs.anchor: Yea, for thy sake are we killed, &c.

paragraphs.text: As those Christians in Calabria, A. D. 1560, thrust up in one house together, as in a sheepfold, and butchered individually; {Rom 8:36} besides those many, whose names being written in red letters of blood in the Church’s calendar, are written in golden letters in Christ’s register in the book of life, as Prudentius hath it.
paragraphs.anchor: We are counted as sheep for the slaughter

paragraphs.text: Considering all the premises, stir up thyself, and come and save us? carest thou not that we perish?
paragraphs.anchor: Awake, why sleepest thou?

paragraphs.text: God sometimes concealeth his love, as Joseph did, out of increasement of love; he retireth, but faith fetcheth him out, as the woman of Canaan did, Mar 7:24-25.
paragraphs.anchor: Wherefore hidest thou thy face?

paragraphs.text: Soul and belly (or body), both are oppressed, and lie suppliant at God’s feet; resolved there to live and die together.
paragraphs.anchor: For our soul, &c.

paragraphs.text: Heb. A help for us, a sufficient help, proportionable to our necessities. The Hebrew hath a letter more than ordinary. {Hebrew Text Note}
paragraphs.anchor: Arise for our help
